Within child contribution “Individualized nutritional approach for individuals with the Flammer syndrome phenotype” (body lines 816–908), green-tea catechins appear in the glaucoma-diet recommendations (line 854); smell/odor disorder is a separate section of the same contribution (lines 846–852). This is not a green-tea intervention or measured olfactory outcome, and the population is Flammer syndrome, not Parkinson disease. Same child, distinct topics; no claim-level result.

“Coffee” appears in the bibliography of the Flammer-nutrition contribution (line 882, a citation on coffee/caffeine and blood pressure). Fatigue occurrences are in other proceedings contributions (e.g., voice fatigue and MS-related fatigue), not in that cited work or a coffee intervention. Collection-level collision; no brewed-coffee/fatigue result.

Ground turmeric/curcuminoids occur in the Flammer-nutrition glaucoma recommendation (line 854). Fall/fall-detection terms belong to the separate biosensing contribution (lines 122–134; includes a hiker/watch anecdote), not a turmeric report. No turmeric/fall endpoint.

Turmeric/curcuminoids occur in the Flammer-nutrition glaucoma passage (line 854). “Rigidity” in the neighboring Flammer pregnancy contribution is vascular rigidity (lines 780–812), not Parkinsonian muscle rigidity; these are separate children and outcomes.

The contribution makes general recommendations, with no turmeric intervention, no measured olfaction outcome, and no Parkinson population.

Full-text review of the original PLoS One article (“Charting the onset of Parkinson-like motor and non-motor symptoms in nonhuman primate model of Parkinson’s disease”) found no lemon balm/Melissa exposure. The study follows MPTP-lesioned marmosets (n=3), with tremor, sleep/circadian, fine-motor, cognitive and behavioral observations; it is not a food study. Local body terms around “to date” and references can create lexical noise; no depressive scale or lemon-balm result.
No fig/fig-fruit exposure and no drooling endpoint in the marmoset paper. The study is an animal PD-model chronology report; it cannot support raw fig or drooling claims.
No dried dates are fed or evaluated. The article describes MPTP-marmoset PD-like motor/nonmotor signs; pain is not a measured outcome for a date intervention. Source context is animal model only.

No raw fig exposure. The full report does measure postural/action/rest tremor in MPTP marmosets using video-based tremor analysis and a Parkinson disease rating scale (PDRS), n=3. This is useful symptom/model context only, not dietary evidence.
No dried-date exposure. Marmosets are described as showing apathy/indifference at follow-up, but no date intervention or food-related apathy outcome is tested; animal PD-model context only.

No fig exposure (the apparent “fig” match is figure/Fig. text). This is a registered human PD feasibility trial of MCT-supplemented ketogenic diet (NCT04584346), not a food/fig trial. Visual hallucinations appear only among patient-perceived week-3 benefits (two participants, Table 7), not as a validated prespecified hallucination-frequency effect.

No date-fruit intervention; “date” occurs in the registration-date text. Daily PD symptom log (Table 6) includes pain ratings on a 0–3 better/normal/worse scale; authors report similar symptoms between diet arms and no significant differences except daily off time. The tested intervention is MCT ketogenic diet, not dates.

No fig exposure; figure labels cause the apparent match. Table 6 includes a daily tremor item, with no significant diet-group difference reported. The study is a short feasibility diet trial, not raw fig exposure.

No date-fruit intervention. The daily symptom survey includes a “unmotivated or lack of desire” item (apathy proxy) and Table 6 reports apathy values; no significant diet-group difference is reported. Diet was MCT ketogenic, not dates.
